question: Can a foreign investor set up a regional holding / head-office company in Indonesia (KBLI 70100) to manage several of my other PT PMAs?
answer: On paper, yes — but with one hard structural catch flagged by our verification data, plus one scoping question to settle. The ownership layer first: KBLI 2025 code **70100 — Head Office Activities** covers strategic oversight, planning, and ACTIVE day-to-day management of other units of your corporate group, and it is not on Indonesia's restricted or closed investment list — so at the classification level it reads as open to full foreign ownership (**TERBUKA, 100%**). The catch: our canonical KBLI/OSS verification dataset records that 70100 carries registration rows only for micro, small and medium enterprises — there is no large-enterprise (Usaha Besar) row for it in OSS, which in practice reserves the code for domestic UMKM-scale operators. A PT PMA is a large enterprise by law, so on that data **a PT PMA cannot actually be registered under 70100 as things stand** — the ownership openness is real on paper, but it is not usable by a foreign-investment company in practice. (Full disclosure: this structural verdict comes from our internal verification dataset and is the same reading shown by public OSS mirrors; it is pending one final re-derivation pass on our side, so we confirm it in writing before you act on it either way.) The scoping question now matters even more: 70100's own official classification scope explicitly EXCLUDES pure equity-holding activity that isn't tied to management services — a company that only OWNS shares in your other PT PMAs, without providing them active management/oversight services, falls under a different code (KBLI 64210, "Holding Company Activities"), which our dataset records as open to full foreign ownership (TERBUKA, 100%) — though we have not separately verified its OSS registrability for a PT PMA in this dossier. So before you structure anything: tell us whether the entity will actively manage the group day-to-day or passively hold shares, and we will confirm the workable classification (an active-management alternative to 70100, or 64210 for a holding structure) and its ownership treatment in writing before you register. Separately, we do need to flag an honest gap on 70100's own licensing citation: it could not be independently confirmed against our pinned copy of the underlying regulation — it isn't that we found it wrong, just that we couldn't verify it, so we've paused on repeating it rather than assert something unconfirmed.

question: I want to open a staffing / labor-placement agency (KBLI 78109) in Bali — can it be foreign-owned, and can I bring foreign staff (TKA) into the business?

On bringing in foreign staff for your own agency's management roles: any foreign employee still goes through the standard RPTKA (foreign-manpower-utilization-plan) approval and work-permit process — that general framework is separate from, and unaffected by, this code's licensing-detail gap.

question: Can a foreigner own and run a vocational secondary school (SMK-type, KBLI 85321) in Indonesia?
answer: No — this one is genuinely closed to foreign investment, for the specific code you're asking about. KBLI 2025 code **85321** is officially titled **"Government General Vocational Secondary School"** (Pendidikan Menengah Kejuruan Umum **Pemerintah**) — the "Government" in the title matters: this classification is definitionally a government-operated institution type, and it is recorded as **fully closed (TERTUTUP, 0% foreign shareholding)**. Because a private PT PMA is, by definition, not a government operator, your actual project — a privately-run vocational secondary school — almost certainly belongs under the SEPARATE private-sector code, **KBLI 85322 ("Private General Vocational Secondary School")**, whose foreign-ownership status we have NOT verified in this dossier and must confirm before you proceed; don't assume it's open just because it's the private counterpart. This is also different again from higher-education branch campuses or international K-12 schools, which sit under yet other codes with their own foreign-investment rules. Tell us exactly what you're building — government partnership, private SMK, foreign branch campus, or international school — and we'll confirm the one applicable code and its ownership status. We also found and removed an unrelated licensing block that had been mistakenly attached to 85321 itself (it described a Special Economic Zone branch-campus higher-education regime, not secondary vocational education) — that correction doesn't change 85321's own 0% ownership answer, but it doesn't resolve the code-routing question above either.

question: Bali Zero told me my KBLI code's licensing status is "pending regulation" — does that mean my planned business is illegal, or that I can't register my company?

It does NOT block you from incorporating your PT PMA or registering your NIB through Indonesia's OSS system — those steps run off your KBLI activity classification and ownership status, both of which are unaffected, for the general case (see Q16 for the one narrow exception: a small number of very-high-risk activities where the NIB step itself can be provisionally affected). What it does mean is that we can't yet hand you a confirmed operational-permit checklist for that specific activity, and we'd rather tell you that than give you one that turns out to be wrong.

question: Someone told me a specific license is required for my KBLI code, but Bali Zero says it's "not yet confirmed" — why the difference, and who's right?
answer: Both of you may be looking at the same underlying government dataset — the issue is that Indonesia's 2025 business-classification update (KBLI 2025) reclassified, merged, or split thousands of activity codes, and in a number of cases the old licensing detail didn't carry forward cleanly onto the new code: it sometimes points to a different, unrelated business activity, or to a classification that no longer exists in its old form. That's a data-quality problem in how the crosswalk was compiled and carried forward — we can't yet say for certain whether it originated in the government's own source data or was introduced during someone's compilation of it, only that it's a compilation issue, not a change in the underlying law. Bali Zero runs a dedicated internal verification pass — checking each citation against the actual regulation text, page by page, rather than trusting the crosswalk at face value — and where we find a mismatch, we say so rather than repeat it. If another source is citing a specific requirement for your code that we've flagged as unconfirmed, we'd treat that citation as unverified until it can be traced to the correct page of the actual regulation — and we're happy to walk through our finding with you or your other advisor directly.

question: What's the difference between "open" (TERBUKA), "restricted" (TERBATAS), and "closed" (TERTUTUP) for foreign ownership, and how do I find out which applies to my code?
answer: These three labels describe the maximum share of your company that foreign investors can own for a given business activity, as set out in Indonesia's positive-investment-list regulation: **TERBUKA (open)** means up to 100% foreign ownership is allowed with no mandatory local partner — code 66123 (digital-asset brokerage) and 70100 (head office) in this dossier are examples. **TERBATAS (restricted)** means foreign ownership is capped below 100% and you need at least one Indonesian shareholder for the remainder — code 50113 (domestic sea tourism transport) in this dossier is an example, capped at 49%. **TERTUTUP (closed)** means the activity is not open to foreign investment at all — code 85321 (public vocational secondary school) in this dossier is an example, at 0%. Every KBLI code has its own answer to this question, and it's one of the first things we check before recommending any structure — tell us your intended activity and we'll confirm the applicable cap for you.
